newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's Old Mutual urges removal of fx controls.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Old Mutual urges removal of fx controls.

text.p: Leading life insurer Old Mutual said on Thursday the full benefits of globalisation would only be felt once exchange controls had been lifted.

Old Mutual chairman Mike Levett told the group's annual general meeting he had welcomed government's decision in June allowing financial institutions to swap 10 percent of total assets with foreign counterparties -- seen as a precursor to the eventual lifting of remaining exchange controls.
"But the benefits and challenges of globalisation will only be fully experienced with the lifting of exchange controls," Levett said.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said recently the lifting of existing exchange controls could take four to five years, but economists have pushed for a speedier lifting.

"Although asset swaps do not represent an ideal mechanism through which South Africans can diversify their savings internationally, they are nonetheless playing a role in enabling some diversification of investments," Levett said.

"While we believe that the lifting of exchange controls will ultimately benefit the South African economy, Old Mutual's expanding international activities are also providing immediate benefit for the South African economy, since several of our key business services are aimed at channeling foreign investment into this country," he added.

For example, the launch of the OMEGA and SAGA funds had given international institutions access to the South African share market. The OMEGA was available to US clients and the SAGA to non-US clients. Both funds combined the liquidity of an open-ended fund with the portfolio stability and reduced trading costs associated with a closed-ended fund.

Other new products included Old Mutual's Worldwide Equity and Worldwide Balanced funds, which had, for the first time in 30 years, given South African investors the opportunity to gain exposure to foreign investments.
In the area of employee benefits, the new International Asset Portfolio had been launched, Levett said.
This was a unitised portfolio consisting of stocks from the Morgan Stanley Capital International World Index. By June this year it had a portfolio of 355 million rand.
Old Mutual had also launched a Global Equity Fund, which had taken "line honours among international unit trusts, providing a 33.4 percent return for the year ended June 30, 1996," Levett said.
But the group was not only concentrating on markets abroad, Levett said. It was firmly established in Namibia, Zimbabwe, Kenya and Malawi and was considering "selective" expansion into other markets.
